title: Alexis of Russia
wiki_lead:
Alexei Mikhailovich (Russian: Алексей Михайлович, IPA: [ɐlʲɪkˈsʲej mʲɪˈxajləvʲɪtɕ]; 19 March [O.S. 9 March] 1629 – 8 February [O.S. 29 January] 1676), also known as Alexis, was Tsar of all Russia from 1645 until his death in 1676. He was the second Russian tsar from the House of Romanov.
He was the first tsar to sign laws on his own authority and his council passed the Sobornoye Ulozheniye of 1649, which strengthened the bonds between autocracy and the lower nobility. In religious matters, he sided closely with Patriarch Nikon during the schism in the Russian Orthodox Church which saw unpopular liturgical reforms.
While finding success in foreign affairs, his reign saw several wars with Iran, Poland (from whom left-bank Ukraine and Smolensk were annexed) and Sweden, as well as internal instabilities such as the Salt Riot in Moscow and the Cossack revolt of Stenka Razin in southern Russia. At the time of his death, Russia spanned almost 8.1 million km2 (3.1 million mi2).

Alexei Mikhailovich (Russian: Алексей Михайлович, IPA: [ɐlʲɪkˈsʲej mʲɪˈxajləvʲɪtɕ]; 19 March [O.S. 9 March] 1629 – 8 February [O.S. 29 January] 1676), also known as Alexis, was Tsar of all Russia from 1645 until his death in 1676. He was the second Russian tsar from the House of Romanov.
He was the first tsar to sign laws on his own authority and his council passed the Sobornoye Ulozheniye of 1649, which strengthened the bonds between autocracy and the lower nobility. In religious matters, he sided closely with Patriarch Nikon during the schism in the Russian Orthodox Church which saw unpopular liturgical reforms.
While finding success in foreign affairs, his reign saw several wars with Iran, Poland (from whom left-bank Ukraine and Smolensk were annexed) and Sweden, as well as internal instabilities such as the Salt Riot in Moscow and the Cossack revolt of Stenka Razin in southern Russia. At the time of his death, Russia spanned almost 8.1 million km2 (3.1 million mi2).


Early life and reign
Alexis was born on 19 March [O.S. 9 March] 1629, in Moscow, to Tsar Michael and Eudoxia Streshneva. At the age of sixteen, he acceded to the throne after his father's death on 12 July 1645. In August, the Tsar's mother died, and following a pilgrimage to Sergiyev Posad he was crowned on 28 September in the Dormition Cathedral. He was committed to the care of his tutor Boris Morozov, a shrewd boyar open to Western ideas.
Morozov pursued a peaceful foreign policy, securing a truce with the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth and carefully avoiding complications with the Ottoman Empire. His domestic policy aimed at limiting the privileges of foreign traders and abolishing useless and expensive court offices. On 17 January 1648, Morozov procured the marriage of the tsar with Maria Miloslavskaya, himself marrying her sister Anna ten days later; both were daughters of Ilya Danilovich Miloslavsky.
Alexis empowered Morozov to conduct reforms to reduce social tensions; however, his measure of tripling the tax burden (arrears for the two years preceding 1648 was demanded) caused heightened popular discontent. Morozov was regarded as a corrupt, self-seeking boyar and was accused of sorcery and witchcraft. In May 1648 Muscovites rose against his faction in the Salt Riot, and the young Tsar was compelled to dismiss them and exile Morozov to the Kirillo-Belozersky Monastery. Four months later, Morozov secretly returned to Moscow to regain some of his power.
The popular discontent demonstrated by the riot was partially responsible for Alexis' 1649 issuance of a new legal code, the Sobornoye Ulozheniye.


Later reign


Military reform
In 1648, using the experience of creating regiments of the foreign system during the reign of his father, Alexis began reforming the army.
The main direction of the reform was the mass creation of New Order Regiments: Reiters, Soldiers, Dragoons and Hussars. These regiments formed the backbone of the new army of Tsar Alexis. To fulfill the reform goals, a large number of European military specialists were hired for service. This became possible because of the end of the Thirty Years' War, which created a colossal surplus of military professionals in Europe.


Rebellions

Throughout his reign, Alexis faced rebellions across Russia. After resolving the 1648 Salt Riot Alexis faced rebellions in 1650 in the cities of Pskov and Great Novgorod. Alexis put down the Novgorod rebellion quickly, but was unable to subdue Pskov, and was forced to promise the city amnesty in return for surrender. The Metropolitan Nikon distinguished himself at Great Novgorod and in 1651 became the Tsar's chief minister.
By the 1660s, Alexis's wars with Poland and Sweden had put an increasing strain on the Russian economy and public finances. In response, Alexis's government had begun minting large numbers of copper coins in 1654 to increase government revenue but this led to a devaluation of the ruble and a severe financial crisis. grok_lead: Alexis Mikhailovich Romanov (19 March 1629 â 8 February 1676) was Tsar of All Russia from 1645 until his death, succeeding his father Michael I as the second monarch of the Romanov dynasty. Born in Moscow to Tsar Michael I and Tsarina Eudoxia Lukyanovna Streshneva, Alexis ascended the throne at the age of sixteen following his father's passing. His reign, spanning over three decades, witnessed the consolidation of autocratic authority through legal codification, military engagements that expanded Russian territory, and profound ecclesiastical divisions. A defining legislative achievement was the promulgation of the Sobornoe Ulozhenie in 1649, a comprehensive law code that eliminated time limits on the recapture of fugitive serfs, effectively entrenching hereditary serfdom and binding peasants more firmly to the land and their lords. This reform addressed fiscal pressures but exacerbated social tensions, contributing to urban uprisings in Moscow and other cities. Militarily, Alexis pursued expansionist policies, notably incorporating the left-bank Ukraine via the Treaty of Pereyaslavl in 1654 with Cossack leader Bohdan Khmelnytsky, which precipitated the protracted Russo-Polish War (1654â1667) and subsequent territorial acquisitions including Kiev and Smolensk under the Armistice of Andrusovo. These gains bolstered Russia's southern frontiers against Crimean Tatar incursions, though they also strained resources and invited internal dissent, exemplified by the Cossack rebellion of Stenka Razin from 1670 to 1671. In religious affairs, Alexis initially championed Patriarch Nikon's liturgical reforms starting in 1652, aimed at aligning Russian Orthodox practices with Byzantine originals, including revisions to service books, the sign of the cross, and processional rites. However, escalating conflicts with Nikon led to the patriarch's deposition by the Great Moscow Synod in 1666, which nonetheless ratified the reforms and anathematized opponents, formalizing the Raskol schism that splintered the church into the state-backed faction and the persecuted Old Believers who rejected the changes as deviations from ancient traditions. Alexis's personal piety, evidenced by his composition of religious texts and patronage of ecclesiastical art, intertwined with these policies, underscoring a conservative worldview that prioritized doctrinal uniformity under tsarist oversight. Twice marriedâfirst to Maria Ilyinichna Miloslavskaya in 1648, by whom he fathered thirteen children including future Tsar Feodor III, and second to Natalya Kirillovna Naryshkina in 1671, mother of Peter the GreatâAlexis's court reflected emerging Western influences, such as the establishment of Russia's first public theater in 1672. He perished from a heart attack at age 46, leaving a legacy of institutional strengthening amid recurrent upheavals that foreshadowed the transformative era of his son Peter.
